questions.q: What does setting runAsNonRoot: true in a Pod's securityContext actually do?
options: It deletes the container's root filesystem
It refuses to start the container at all if its image tries to run as UID 0
It grants the container extra Linux capabilities
It only affects logging, not runtime behavior
questions.explain: runAsNonRoot: true causes the kubelet to refuse starting the container if its image attempts to run as the root user (UID 0).

questions.q: Which Pod Security Standard represents current hardening best practice, including settings like allowPrivilegeEscalation: false and dropping all capabilities?
options: privileged
baseline
restricted
there is no such standard; it must be configured manually every time
questions.explain: Of the three built-in Pod Security Standards, restricted is the strictest and encodes current Pod hardening best practice.

questions.q: What is the effect of labeling a namespace with pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted?
options: It only logs a warning; non-compliant Pods still run
The API server rejects any Pod submitted to that namespace that doesn't meet the restricted profile, before it's ever scheduled
It applies only to Deployments, not plain Pods
It deletes any existing non-compliant Pods automatically
questions.explain: The enforce label makes Pod Security Admission actively reject non-compliant Pod submissions at the namespace level, rather than merely warning.

questions.q: Why does readOnlyRootFilesystem: true matter for a container that is compromised through a dependency vulnerability?
options: It prevents the container from starting at all
It stops the attacker from writing new files (like a malicious binary) outside of explicitly mounted volumes
It encrypts all network traffic from the container
It automatically restarts the container every time it is written to
questions.explain: A read-only root filesystem denies writes anywhere except explicitly provided volumes, limiting what an attacker inside a compromised container can do, such as dropping new executables.

questions.q: Why enforce Pod Security at the namespace level (via Pod Security Admission) rather than relying on each Pod's own YAML to set securityContext correctly?
options: Namespace-level enforcement is faster at runtime
It removes the possibility that an individual Pod spec forgets or deliberately omits the hardening settings, since the API server rejects non-compliant Pods regardless of who wrote the YAML
securityContext fields are ignored unless set at the namespace level
It is required before any RBAC Role can be created
questions.explain: Namespace-level enforcement guarantees a floor that applies to every Pod submitted to that namespace, closing the gap where a single mistaken or malicious Pod spec could bypass hardening.
